analysis.one_liner: Ends visitor fees at federal recreation sites and charges miners a royalty to pay for park upkeep.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House Resources subcommittee from November 13, 1997 until the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999. [S5]
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have done two things at once: repealed the 1996 pilot program that charges visitors fees at national parks, forests and other federal recreation sites, and created a 5% royalty on gold, silver, copper and other hardrock minerals mined from federal land under the 1872 general mining law. Hardrock miners pay no royalty today, unlike oil, gas and coal companies on federal leases. The royalty money would have gone straight to public recreation — 70% to the National Park Service, 20% to the Forest Service, 6% to the Bureau of Land Management, 3% to the Fish and Wildlife Service and 1% for administration — to pay down the repair backlog and fund upkeep, signage, habitat work and law enforcement at those sites. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Visitors to national parks, forests and other federal recreation lands, who would stop paying the pilot fees; and taxpayers generally, who would finally collect something for hardrock minerals taken from public land. Users of those sites would also gain from royalty-funded repairs, signage, habitat work and law enforcement. [S2][S3]

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the recreational fee demonstration program created by a 1996 appropriations act, ending the pilot fees charged to visitors at federal recreation sites.

Charges producers of hardrock minerals from federal mining claims a royalty of 5% of net smelter return — the minerals outside the federal leasing system that already charges royalties on oil, gas and coal.

Dedicates every royalty dollar to public recreation without further appropriation: 70% to the National Park Service, 20% to the Forest Service, 6% to the Bureau of Land Management, 3% to the Fish and Wildlife Service, and 1% for Interior's administrative costs, spent on backlogged repairs (including health and safety), interpretation, signage, habitat and facility enhancement, operations, and law enforcement.
Requires quarterly reporting and authorizes audits of mining-claim holders, with civil penalties up to $10,000 for knowingly false or missing information.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies producing from federal mining claims: 5% of net smelter return, quarterly reporting, possible audits, and civil penalties up to $10,000 for false or missing reports. Some of that cost could reach consumers and mining towns through prices and production decisions. [S3]

drawbacks.text: A 5% royalty would raise the cost of mining on federal land, and marginal operations could become uneconomic — a real cost for towns built around those jobs.
Repealing the fee program would remove an existing funding stream before anyone knows whether royalty revenue would replace it; mineral royalties rise and fall with commodity prices and production.
Dedicating the receipts 'without further appropriation' takes the money out of Congress's normal annual budget process, weakening oversight of how it is spent.
The bill is a narrow fix: it adds a royalty but leaves the rest of the 1872 general mining law untouched, including claims and patent provisions long criticized as outdated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the trade is favorable and easy to state: the cost of visiting public land goes down, and the repair backlog at parks and forests is paid by an industry that currently pays nothing for the minerals it removes from public ground. The real costs fall on mining companies and, at the margin, on mining jobs and consumer prices if marginal mines close. The design is modest rather than sweeping — a 5% rate is low by federal-lease standards, the earmarking skips the annual appropriations process, and repealing the fee program before proving the royalty can cover the gap is a genuine gamble. But the core exchange — visitor fees out, mining royalties in — is simple and favors the public.

outcome.mechanism: It died in committee: two weeks after introduction it was sent to the Resources Committee's Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, and it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on November 5, 1997, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources the same day.
On November 13, 1997, the committee requested an executive comment from the Interior Department and referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources.
No further action was recorded for the rest of the 105th Congress, which ended January 3, 1999 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies, which kept removing gold, silver and other minerals from federal land without paying a royalty, and the fee program the bill targeted stayed in place, so visitors kept paying. [S3][S5]

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 5, 1997, pairing repeal of public-land recreation fees with a hardrock mining royalty to fund park and forest upkeep.

for.name: 10 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill during the 105th Congress; original cosponsors included Furse, Markey, Stark, Frank of Massachusetts, Maloney of New York, Hooley and Luther.

against.name: House Committee on Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on November 5, 1997 and never reported it; the bill was referred to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on November 13, 1997 and saw no hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Companies mining gold, silver and other locatable minerals under the 1872 general mining law
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal royalties on hardrock mining throughout the 1990s debates over rewriting the 1872 mining law.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 10 of 10 — and the bill never advanced out of committee. [S4][S5]

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, silver, copper and other locatable minerals on federal land)
industries.note: These companies take minerals from federal claims under the 1872 general mining law without paying any royalty — the only major extractive use of federal land that carries none. The bill would charge them 5% of net smelter return plus reporting and audit compliance, converting that free ride into public revenue earmarked for recreation.
